# Preface {.unnumbered}

Most research code is not a homework hand-in. It grows for months or years: new
dependencies, shared repos, experiments you need to reproduce, and collaborators
who were not in the room when you wrote the first script. Yet many students arrive
with experience only from introductory programming or algorithms courses — a few
files, a single deadline, no version control, no package layout, and no plan for
what happens after the grade is posted.

Robotics and robot learning add a second gap. The **ecosystem is fragmented**:
MuJoCo next to Isaac/Omniverse, URDF/MJCF next to USD, ROS-adjacent tooling next
to bare Python repos, `conda` next to `uv`, sim next to real hardware — and every
lab picks a different slice. People entering from mechanical engineering, EE,
computer science, or ML rarely share the same baseline; some have never opened a
terminal outside a notebook. Excellent **courses** exist, but they usually **teach
the science, not the workshop**. A typical university robotics class covers models
and control; open RL courses such as [Berkeley CS285](http://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse/) go deep on policies, value functions, and sample complexity — not on editable installs, git hygiene, why your quaternion convention disagrees with the sim, or which contact model your stack assumes. The result is talented students who can derive a Bellman backup but stall on “clone this repo, sync the env, and get `step()` to run headless on the cluster.”

This tutorial fills both gaps. It is onboarding for the `robotics` example package
and, more broadly, for **how to start, develop, organize, and maintain a research
project in practice**: Python environments and imports, project structure,
debugging, version control, NumPy/PyTorch tensor work, and the robotics concepts
(kinematics, rotations, simulators, IK, contact models) that `src/robotics/`
illustrates. It does **not** replace an RL or controls course — it gives you a
**single coherent path** through the engineering layer those courses usually skip,
so you can actually run experiments, compare simulators sensibly, and collaborate
without re-learning the stack every rotation. The tone is closer to [MIT's *The Missing Semester*](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/) than to a language syntax cheat sheet — tools and habits you use every week, not once on an exam.

We deliberately stay **narrow and runnable** rather than cataloguing every framework.
One small repo, two simulators on the same MJCF, one IK registry — enough structure
to transfer when your lab switches to Isaac, ROS 2, or a custom GPU env. When you
outgrow this book, use [References and external docs](references.qmd#references)
for official install guides and APIs; use your RL/control coursework for the math.

The book is split into short, self-contained chapters so sections can be edited
and reviewed independently. Use the sidebar to navigate.

## How to use it

- The runnable examples live in `scripts/` and the library in `src/robotics/`.
  Set the environment up once with `uv sync`, then run any example with
  `uv run python scripts/<name>.py`.
- Code blocks in these pages are illustrative snippets; the authoritative,
  runnable versions are the files under `scripts/` and `src/`.
- **External links:** standards (PEPs), install guides, and simulator docs are
  collected in [References and external docs](references.qmd#references). Chapters
  link there or inline where a tool is first introduced.
- **Progress:** each major section (`##` heading) has a **Done** checkbox. Your
  choices are saved in this browser only (`localStorage`). Unread sections are
  highlighted in the page table of contents; **red `!`** marks warning sections
  (footguns and `.common-bug-warning` callouts) not yet marked done; the left
  sidebar shows chapter status (blue = not finished, orange = partly done, ✓ =
  all sections on that chapter marked done).

## Building these docs

```bash
uv sync                 # project env (numpy, einops)
quarto preview docs     # live-reloading local preview
quarto render docs      # build static HTML into docs/_site
```

Install the [Quarto CLI](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) separately (not a Python package). See [References](references.qmd#version-control-and-publishing) for other tool install links.
